title: 2027-28 FAFSA: Why Over $1,500 of Savings Interest Can Make Your Balances Count
description: Under $60,000 AGI, one FAFSA asset exemption requires no Schedule B, needed past $1,500 of taxable interest or ordinary dividends. What counts at 12% and 20%.
content:
A parent sitting down this month to fill in the 2027-28 FAFSA for a high school senior usually has two questions about the family's savings: will the form ask about them at all, and if it does, how much will they count? The short answer comes from the federal statute. Under its income-and-schedules test, a dependent student's family with parents' adjusted gross income under $60,000 skips asset reporting only if the parents did not file Schedule A, B, D, E, F or H (and either filed no Schedule C or filed one within a $10,000 gain or loss) with the return for the second preceding tax year, and the IRS requires Schedule B once taxable interest or ordinary dividends go over $1,500. A well-funded high-yield savings account can produce that much interest on its own. (Two other routes to the exemption, covered below, do not depend on tax schedules.) Once assets are in the picture, the statute counts parents' assets above an asset protection allowance at 12%, and that figure is then added to the parents' income and assessed again. A dependent student's assets count at 20% and go straight into the Student Aid Index. For 2027-28 the asset protection allowance, which the statute's base table sets above zero for most parent ages, is $0 at every age.

None of that tells a family what its aid will be. It does explain which balances belong on the form, whose name each one goes under, and why a savings account that throws off a few extra hundred dollars of interest can change which questions get asked. The rules below come from the Federal Student Aid announcement, three sections of the Higher Education Act as printed in the U.S. Code 2024 edition, the Department of Education's June 2, 2026 notice and the IRS instructions for Schedule B.

## The 2027-28 FAFSA is open now

Federal Student Aid posted its announcement, [2027–28 FAFSA Form Now Available](https://financialaidtoolkit.ed.gov/tk/announcement-detail.jsp?id=fafsa-updates), on its Financial Aid Toolkit with a date stamp of Sept. 23, 2026. The announcement says students "can complete the form to apply for financial aid for attending college or career/trade school between July 1, 2027, and June 30, 2028." That window is the 2027-28 award year, and it is the reference point for every date-based rule that follows.

Two other lines from the announcement matter for families who started early. Students who "successfully submitted their FAFSA form for the 2027–28 academic year during the early testing period" do not need to resubmit it. And on timing, the announcement says "Most FAFSA forms are processed immediately. Some can take one to three days." Once a form is processed, the student can review the FAFSA Submission Summary, and the information goes to the schools the student selected.

The award year matters because the statute does not look at this year's tax return. In the need analysis definitions at [20 U.S.C. 1087vv](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-2024-title20/html/USCODE-2024-title20-chap28-subchapIV-partF-sec1087vv.htm), "total income" is built from "adjusted gross income for the second preceding tax year," and the asset-reporting exemption uses the same phrase for the tax schedules a family filed. Counting back two years from an award year that begins July 1, 2027 points to the 2025 tax year. The Schedule B instructions quoted later in this post are the IRS's 2025 instructions, the ones that applied to 2025 returns.

So the form uses two different reference points. Income, and the tax-schedule test for skipping asset questions, come from a past return. Account balances and other asset values, when they are asked about at all, are measured at a different point: "the market value at the time of application," in the words of the statute. The income figures are fixed in the past, while account balances can change until the day the form is completed.

## Who is exempt from asset reporting

The exemption lives in [20 U.S.C. 1087ss](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-2024-title20/html/USCODE-2024-title20-chap28-subchapIV-partF-sec1087ss.htm), subsection (b). It opens with this instruction: "the Secretary shall not use asset information from an eligible applicant or, as applicable, the parent or spouse of an eligible applicant." The rest of the subsection defines who counts as an eligible applicant. An applicant needs to meet only one of the criteria.

For a dependent student, three of them apply:

1. **Automatic zero or negative SAI.** The applicant "qualifies for an automatic zero student aid index or negative student aid index" under another section of the law, 20 U.S.C. 1087mm. The income tests in that section are outside the scope of this post.
2. **The income-and-schedules test.** The student's parents "have a total adjusted gross income (excluding any income of the dependent student) that is less than $60,000 and do not file a Schedule A, B, D, E, F, or H (or equivalent successor schedules) with the Federal income tax return for the second preceding tax year." On top of that, the parents either do not file a Schedule C for that year, or they file one "with net business income of not more than a $10,000 loss or gain."
3. **A means-tested benefit.** The applicant, or the applicant's parent or spouse as applicable, "at any time during the previous 24-month period, received a benefit under a means-tested Federal benefit program."

The statute's list of means-tested programs includes Supplemental Security Income, SNAP, TANF, WIC, Medicaid and federal housing assistance, plus other programs the Secretary finds approximately consistent with their income eligibility rules.

There is one carve-out that cuts the other way. Under paragraph (3), a dependent student's family is not exempt if the parents do not "reside in the United States or a United States territory" or do not "file taxes in the United States or a United States territory," unless the nonfiling happens because the parents were not required to file "due to a low income."

The second criterion involves more than the $60,000 figure. The statute defines each schedule by what it reports:

| Schedule | What the statute says it reports | Effect on the test |
|---|---|---|
| A | Itemized deductions | Rules it out |
| B | Interest and ordinary dividend income | Rules it out |
| C | Income or loss from a business or profession run as a sole proprietor | Allowed only within a $10,000 loss or gain |
| D | Sales, exchanges or some involuntary conversions of capital assets, certain capital gain distributions, nonbusiness bad debts | Rules it out |
| E | Income from rental properties, royalties, partnerships, S corporations, estates, trusts and residual interests in real estate mortgage investment conduits | Rules it out |
| F | Farm income and expenses | Rules it out |
| H | Household employment taxes | Rules it out |

Any one of these schedules is enough to fail the test. A family with AGI well under $60,000 that itemized deductions, sold some shares, reported rental income on Schedule E, or paid a household employee can fail this test for reasons that have nothing to do with savings. A family that tripped none of those can still fail it on Schedule B alone. Meeting one of the other criteria, such as a means-tested benefit in the previous 24 months, would still qualify the family, because one criterion is enough.

## How Schedule B gets triggered at $1,500

The IRS sets the Schedule B filing rules in its [Instructions for Schedule B (Form 1040)](https://www.irs.gov/instructions/i1040sb). The 2025 instructions list several situations that require the schedule. The first is the one that matters for savers: "You had over $1,500 of taxable interest or ordinary dividends."

Two words in that sentence matter most. "Over" means a family with exactly $1,500 of taxable interest is not caught by that line; the schedule is required once the amount goes past it. And "taxable interest" is the total that appears on the return, from every account that paid it, added up. The sentence does not set a separate line for each account. A family with three modest accounts at three banks can cross the line even though no single 1099-INT looks large. For couples who hold a joint account, how that interest is reported on a return is covered in [Joint Savings Account, One 1099-INT: Who Reports the Interest and How](https://smartmoneydaily.github.io/2026/09/30/joint-savings-account-one-1099-int-who-reports-the-interest-and-how/).

The $1,500 line is not the only route onto Schedule B. The same instructions list other triggers, and a few of them show up in college-saving households:

- Interest received from a seller-financed mortgage where the buyer used the property as a personal residence.
- Accrued interest from a bond.
- Claiming "the exclusion of interest from series EE or I U.S. savings bonds issued after 1989." A family that claimed that exclusion on a 2025 return filed Schedule B for that reason.
- Receiving interest or ordinary dividends as a nominee.
- Having "a financial interest in, or signature authority over, a financial account in a foreign country," or a connection to a foreign trust as the instructions describe.

Any one of them means a Schedule B was part of the return, and the statute's test asks only whether the parents filed one.

The connection to the FAFSA is the statute's own definition. Section 1087ss(b)(4)(B) says "The term 'Schedule B' means a form or information filed by a taxpayer to report interest and ordinary dividend income." Read together, the two documents connect like this: more than $1,500 of taxable interest in 2025 meant a Schedule B on the 2025 return, and a Schedule B on that return removes the second criterion for skipping asset reporting on the 2027-28 FAFSA, even if the parents' AGI was below $60,000.

## How much savings produces $1,500 of interest

The interest figure is a product of two things: the balance and the yield. The table below shows the balance needed to cross $1,500 at several assumed yields.

Here is the arithmetic, using assumed round yields chosen only to show the math, not quotes for any real account. Annual percentage yield already folds in compounding, so a balance held for a full year at a stated APY earns that percentage of the balance.

| Assumed APY, held all year | Balance that earns exactly $1,500 | What it takes to go "over $1,500" |
|---|---|---|
| 2% | $75,000 | Any balance above $75,000 |
| 3% | $50,000 | Any balance above $50,000 |
| 4% | $37,500 | Any balance above $37,500 |
| 5% | $30,000 | Any balance above $30,000 |

Each row is $1,500 divided by the yield: $1,500 ÷ 0.02 = $75,000, $1,500 ÷ 0.03 = $50,000, $1,500 ÷ 0.04 = $37,500 and $1,500 ÷ 0.05 = $30,000. Real accounts rarely sit at one balance and one rate for 12 months, so the actual interest on a 1099-INT can differ from a simple calculation. The point of the table is scale: an emergency fund and a down payment kept in one high-yield account can produce more than $1,500 of interest a year.

**Worked example: one account versus two.** Take a married couple filing jointly with 2025 AGI of $54,000 who filed no other schedules. Assume they kept $40,000 in an online savings account paying an assumed 4% APY for all of 2025.

- Interest: $40,000 × 0.04 = $1,600.
- $1,600 is over $1,500, so the 2025 instructions required Schedule B.
- Under 20 U.S.C. 1087ss(b)(2)(B), filing Schedule B means the second criterion is not met. AGI under $60,000 does not cure it.

Now change one fact. Suppose the same couple held $28,000 in that account at the same assumed 4% APY.

- Interest: $28,000 × 0.04 = $1,120.
- $1,120 is not over $1,500, so the interest line alone did not require Schedule B.
- If nothing else on the 2025 return required Schedule B or any of the other listed schedules, and their AGI stayed under $60,000, the second criterion could be met, and under the statute the Secretary "shall not use asset information" from that family.

The same logic covers interest spread over several accounts. If the couple instead had $18,000 at an assumed 4% and $9,000 in a CD at an assumed 3%, the interest is $18,000 × 0.04 + $9,000 × 0.03 = $720 + $270 = $990, still under the line. What matters for Schedule B is the total on the return.

For the 2027-28 form, the 2025 return is already filed, so the useful step is to read it: whether a Schedule B was attached, and why. Low AGI alone does not settle the question.

## What the statute counts as an asset

When asset information is used, the definition is broad. Section 1087vv(f)(1) says "assets" means "the amount in checking and savings accounts, time deposits, money market funds, investments, trusts, stocks, bonds, derivatives, securities, mutual funds, tax shelters, qualified education benefits (except as provided in paragraph (3)), the annual amount of child support received and the net value of real estate, vacation homes, income producing property, and business and farm assets." One exclusion follows in paragraph (2): "the term 'assets' shall not include the net value of the family's principal place of residence."

Sorted into the categories a saver would recognize, the list looks like this:

| Category | Items the statute names | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Cash and deposits | Checking and savings accounts, time deposits, money market funds | Time deposits include CDs |
| Market investments | Investments, stocks, bonds, derivatives, securities, mutual funds | Net value, per subsection (g) |
| Trusts and shelters | Trusts, tax shelters | Named directly in the definition |
| Education savings | Qualified education benefits: 529 plans, state prepaid tuition plans, Coverdell education savings accounts | Whose asset depends on paragraph (3) |
| Child support | The annual amount of child support received | Listed as an asset, not as a balance |
| Property | Real estate, vacation homes, income producing property | Net value: market value minus debt |
| Home | The family's principal place of residence | Excluded |

**Time deposits.** The Federal Reserve's Regulation D, at [12 CFR 204.2](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-12/chapter-II/subchapter-A/part-204/section-204.2), defines a time deposit as one the depositor cannot withdraw from within six days of deposit unless the deposit carries an early withdrawal penalty of at least seven days' simple interest on the amount withdrawn, and says it may be represented by a certificate. A CD fits that description, so a CD ladder built for a tuition bill is an asset on the same footing as a savings account. Locking money up for a term does not change that.

**Child support.** The definition counts "the annual amount of child support received." That is unusual: it treats a stream of payments as an asset item. A parent who receives child support should expect the annual amount to be part of the asset picture when assets are reported.

This post does not cover how a small business or family farm is valued; the statute quoted here is the U.S. Code 2024 edition, and the treatment of those assets should be checked in the current FAFSA instructions. Retirement accounts and custodial accounts for minors are also outside the scope of this post. Families with any of those should look to the current FAFSA instructions or a school's financial aid office.

## Whose asset a 529 plan is

Paragraph (3) of the definition answers a common question: whose name does a 529 balance go under? The statute says a qualified education benefit "shall be considered an asset of— (A) the student if the student is an independent student; or (B) the parent if the student is a dependent student and the account is designated for the student, regardless of whether the owner of the account is the student or the parent."

Paragraph (4) defines a qualified education benefit as "a qualified tuition program (as defined in section 529(b)(1)(A) of title 26) or other prepaid tuition plan offered by a State" and "a Coverdell education savings account (as defined in section 530(b)(1) of title 26)."

For a dependent student, then:

- A 529 owned by a parent, with the student as the designated beneficiary, is a parent asset.
- A 529 owned by the student, with the student as beneficiary, is also a parent asset under the statute's wording, "regardless of whether the owner of the account is the student or the parent."
- The same rules apply to a state prepaid tuition plan and a Coverdell account.

For an independent student, a qualified education benefit is the student's asset.

The paragraph is specific about what it covers: an account "designated for the student," owned by the student or the parent. It does not address, in that text, an account a parent holds for a different child or an account owned by someone other than the student or a parent. Families with those arrangements should check the current FAFSA guidance or ask the aid office rather than assume.

The classification matters because parent and student assets run through different formulas, covered two sections below.

## Net value, measured at the time of application

The statute does not ask for a year-end statement or an average balance. Section 1087vv(g) defines "net value" as "the market value at the time of application of the assets (as defined in subsection (f)), minus the outstanding liabilities or indebtedness against the assets."

**Timing.** For accounts, investments and property, the net value is measured as things stand when the form is completed, not from a tax return and not from last December's statement. Balances move daily and investments move with prices, so those figures are the ones on the day the form is filled in. The income side of the form looks back to 2025; account balances and market values are taken as of the application date. Child support is the one item in the definition stated differently, as "the annual amount of child support received," so it is an annual figure rather than a balance on that day.

**Debts against an asset.** Net value subtracts "the outstanding liabilities or indebtedness against the assets." The plainest example is real estate other than the home. Assume a family owns a vacation cabin with a market value of $240,000 and an outstanding mortgage of $150,000 on it.

- Net value: $240,000 − $150,000 = $90,000.
- That $90,000 is the asset figure, not the $240,000 sale value.

The definition pairs each debt with the asset it is "against." It does not describe subtracting general household debts from the total. Families unsure whether a particular loan counts as indebtedness against a particular asset can check the current FAFSA instructions. The statute's rule is a measurement date, and the figures reported should be the true values on that date.

## The 12% and 20% rates, and a $0 protection allowance

The assessment rules sit in [20 U.S.C. 1087oo](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-2024-title20/html/USCODE-2024-title20-chap28-subchapIV-partF-sec1087oo.htm), the section that determines the Student Aid Index for a dependent student.

For parents, subsection (d) says "the parents' available assets are equal to— (i) the difference between the parents' assets and the asset protection allowance (determined in accordance with paragraph (2)); multiplied by (ii) 12 percent." It adds that the result "shall not be less than zero."

For the student, subsection (h) says "The student's assets are determined by calculating the assets of the student and multiplying such amount by 20 percent, except that the result shall not be less than zero."

The two numbers do not land in the same place. Subsection (a) builds a dependent student's SAI from three pieces: "the assessment of the parents' adjusted available income," "the assessment of the student's available income," and "the student's available assets." Under subsection (b), the parents' 12% figure is added to the parents' available income to form adjusted available income, and that combined amount then runs through an assessment schedule. The student's 20% figure goes into the SAI directly as its own piece.

The statute's base table for the asset protection allowance rises with the age of the older parent, but the Secretary revises it each year. The Department of Education's notice for this award year, [Federal Need Analysis Methodology for the 2027-28 Award Year](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/06/02/2026-10986/federal-need-analysis-methodology-for-the-2027-28-award-year-federal-pell-grant-federal-work-study), published in the Federal Register on June 2, 2026, describes the allowance as one that "protects a portion of NW (assets less debts) from being considered available for postsecondary educational expenses." Its table for parents of dependent students and for independent students lists every age, from "25 or less" through "65 or older," with an allowance of 0 for married and 0 for single. The notice also describes adjusted available income as "a measure of a family's financial strength, which considers both income and assets."

With the allowance at $0, the parent formula for 2027-28 reduces to parents' assets × 12%. No first slice of savings is shielded by age.

**Worked example: parent and student assets.** Assume a dependent student's parents report, on the day they complete the form, a $4,000 checking balance, $38,000 in savings, a $10,000 CD and a $22,000 529 plan with the student as beneficiary. The student has $3,000 in a savings account of their own.

| Item | Whose asset | Amount |
|---|---|---|
| Checking | Parent | $4,000 |
| Savings | Parent | $38,000 |
| CD (time deposit) | Parent | $10,000 |
| 529 plan designated for the student | Parent, under 1087vv(f)(3) | $22,000 |
| Parents' assets | | $74,000 |
| Student's savings | Student | $3,000 |

The arithmetic:

- Parents: ($74,000 − $0 allowance) × 0.12 = $8,880 in parents' available assets. That $8,880 is added to the parents' available income to form adjusted available income, which is then assessed under the schedule in the June 2 notice.
- Student: $3,000 × 0.20 = $600 in student's available assets, which enters the SAI directly.

Per $1,000: $1,000 of parent assets adds $1,000 × 0.12 = $120 to adjusted available income, while $1,000 of student assets adds $1,000 × 0.20 = $200 directly to the SAI. The $120 is not the end of the parent calculation. The June 2 notice assesses adjusted available income at 22% from −$8,900 to $22,600, rising in steps to 47% on the amount over $45,600, and sets a flat −$1,958 below −$8,900. For a family whose adjusted available income sits in the 22% band, the $120 becomes $120 × 0.22 = $26.40; in the 47% band it becomes $120 × 0.47 = $56.40. This post does not translate the parents' $8,880 into a final SAI, because that depends on the family's income, taxes and allowances, none of which are part of this example.

## Reporting accurately on the day you complete the form

A parent filling in the 2027-28 form can work through the asset questions in this order.

**Check the exemption first, using the 2025 return.** Look at the parents' 2025 federal return. Was AGI under $60,000? Was any Schedule A, B, D, E, F or H attached? Was a Schedule C attached, and if so, was net business income within a $10,000 loss or gain? Separately, did the student or a parent receive a benefit from one of the listed means-tested programs at any time in the previous 24 months? Meeting any one criterion is enough under the statute, unless the paragraph (3) rule for parents who live or file taxes outside the United States applies.

**If Schedule B is there, find out why.** The reason might be interest over $1,500, ordinary dividends over $1,500, a savings bond interest exclusion, a foreign account, or another trigger from the IRS list. Whatever the reason, for this exemption route what matters is whether the parents filed the schedule.

**List every account by owner.** Checking, savings, money market funds, CDs, brokerage holdings, trusts, 529 plans and Coverdell accounts. Put each one under the parent or the student according to the statute's rules, with a dependent student's 529 under the parent.

**Use values from the day of completion.** Pull balances and market values on the day the form is filled in. For property other than the home, subtract only the debt against that property.

Two cautions. First, nothing here is a reason to move money around before completing the form; the statute's job is to measure what a family has, and the figures belong on the form as they are. Second, the documents read for this post cover the federal formula only. For anything a particular school or state program asks for, check with that school's financial aid office.

## Common questions

**Our AGI was under $60,000. Why is the FAFSA still asking about our savings?**

Income below $60,000 is only half of the second criterion in 20 U.S.C. 1087ss(b). The parents also must not have filed Schedule A, B, D, E, F or H with the 2025 return, and any Schedule C must show net business income within a $10,000 loss or gain. A Schedule B filed because taxable interest went over $1,500 is enough to fail that test. The family could still be exempt through another criterion, such as an automatic zero SAI or receipt of a listed means-tested benefit in the previous 24 months.

**Does a 529 plan count against a dependent student more than a parent's savings account?**

No. Under 20 U.S.C. 1087vv(f)(3), a 529 designated for a dependent student counts as a parent asset, "regardless of whether the owner of the account is the student or the parent." That puts it in the same 12% parent formula as the parents' checking, savings and CDs. For 2027-28, with the asset protection allowance at $0, the whole net balance goes into that calculation. The 20% student rate applies to assets that are the student's own, which under the statute does not include that 529.

**Which balance should we report: today's, or the one on our year-end statement?**

The statute defines net value as "the market value at the time of application" minus debts against the asset. That points to the values on the day the form is completed, not a December statement or the interest figures on a tax return. Balances change with deposits, withdrawals and market prices, so pull them on the day you fill in the form.

**Is the family home counted?**

No. Section 1087vv(f)(2) says assets "shall not include the net value of the family's principal place of residence." Other real estate is a different matter: vacation homes, other real estate and income producing property are listed as assets at net value. Net value is market value minus the outstanding debt against that property. Mortgage debt on the principal residence does not enter the asset figure, because the home itself is excluded.

**What is the asset protection allowance for 2027-28?**

It is $0. The Department of Education's notice published June 2, 2026 lists an allowance of 0 for both married and single parents at every age from "25 or less" through "65 or older." The same single table applies to parents of dependent students and to independent students. With a $0 allowance, the statutory parent formula becomes parents' assets × 12%, with a floor of zero.

**Where does the 2025 tax year come from, if the form is for 2027-28?**

The statute bases income and the tax-schedule test on the "second preceding tax year." The 2027-28 award year covers attendance from July 1, 2027 through June 30, 2028, according to the Federal Student Aid announcement. Counting back two years from 2027 gives 2025. That is why the relevant Schedule B rule is the IRS's 2025 instruction about taxable interest or ordinary dividends over $1,500.

title: Medicare Savings Programs: The $9,950 Resource Limit and What Counts
description: Medicare Savings Programs can pay the $202.90 Part B premium. See the 2026 $9,950 and $14,910 resource limits, what counts, and why to apply anyway.
content:
A retiree living mostly on a monthly Social Security check, with about $8,000 spread across checking and savings, sits down before [Medicare Open Enrollment](https://www.medicare.gov/basics/get-started-with-medicare/get-more-coverage/joining-a-plan) to review Medicare costs and assumes that savings balance rules out any help with the Part B premium. Under the 2026 federal figures, the ones Medicare.gov lists now, it does not, at least not by itself. The resource limit for the three Medicare Savings Programs that pay Part B premiums is $9,950 for an individual and $14,910 for a married couple, according to [Medicare.gov's Medicare Savings Programs page](https://www.medicare.gov/basics/costs/help/medicare-savings-programs), and a person whose counted resources are below that line, and whose income is below a separate monthly limit, can qualify to have the state pay the [$202.90 monthly Part B premium](https://www.medicare.gov/basics/costs/medicare-costs).

Two details change the picture for many households. First, not everything you own counts. Medicare lists money in checking, savings and retirement accounts, plus stocks and bonds, as counted resources, but says states don't count your home, one car, a burial plot, up to $1,500 you have set aside for burial expenses, furniture, or other household and personal items. Second, the federal figures are not the last word. Medicare says you may still qualify in your state even if your income or resources are higher than the federal limits, because some states don't count certain types or amounts of income or resources.

In practice: add up only what counts, compare it with $9,950 or $14,910, and if you are close or even somewhat over, apply through your state anyway. Medicare's instruction on this is direct: "Even if you don't think you qualify, you should still apply." Getting into any of the three Part B programs also brings [Extra Help](https://www.medicare.gov/basics/costs/help/drug-costs) with prescription drug costs automatically, which has its own, higher resource limit of $18,090 for an individual and $36,100 for a married couple.

## What a Medicare Savings Program pays for

A Medicare Savings Program, or MSP, is help from your state with Medicare costs. The Medicare page puts it simply: these programs help pay Part A and Part B premiums, and for some people they "might also pay your Part A and Part B deductibles, coinsurance, and copayments." You don't apply through Medicare. You apply through your state, and the state decides which program, if any, you qualify for.

There are four programs, and they differ in what they pay and whom they serve.

| Program | What it helps pay for | Who it is for |
|---|---|---|
| Qualified Medicare Beneficiary (QMB) | Part A premiums (if you don't have premium-free Part A); Part B premiums, deductibles, coinsurance and copayments for services and items Medicare covers | People under the QMB income and resource limits |
| Specified Low-Income Medicare Beneficiary (SLMB) | Part B premiums only | People with both Part A and Part B under the SLMB limits |
| Qualifying Individual (QI) | Part B premiums | People with both Part A and Part B who don't qualify for any other Medicaid coverage or benefits |
| Qualified Disabled & Working Individual (QDWI) | Part A premiums only | People with a disability who are working and lost Social Security disability benefits and premium-free Part A because they returned to work |

For most retirees reviewing their budget, the line that matters is the Part B premium. Medicare's costs page lists the 2026 standard Part B premium as $202.90 each month, "or higher depending on your income," and notes that the amount can change each year. QMB, SLMB and QI all help with that premium. QDWI does not; it is a Part A program for a specific group of working people with disabilities.

QMB goes further than the other two. If you qualify for QMB, Medicare says providers "aren't allowed to bill you for services and items Medicare covers, including deductibles, coinsurance, and copayments." The page adds that you may get a bill for a small Medicaid copayment if one applies, and it tells QMB enrollees to show both their Medicare card and their Medicaid card (or QMB card) each time they get care. People in Original Medicare can also show a Medicare Summary Notice, the claims statement, because it shows they are in the QMB program.

That billing protection is the reason the QMB line in the table carries so much weight. A Part B premium is a known monthly cost. Total spending on deductibles, coinsurance and copayments depends on the care you end up receiving, so for someone with a fixed income it can be the harder part of the budget to predict.

## The 2026 federal income and resource limits

Each program has two tests: a monthly income limit and a resource limit. Here are the 2026 federal figures as Medicare publishes them.

| Program | Monthly income limit, individual | Monthly income limit, married couple | Resource limit, individual | Resource limit, married couple |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| QMB | $1,350 | $1,824 | $9,950 | $14,910 |
| SLMB | $1,616 | $2,184 | $9,950 | $14,910 |
| QI | $1,816 | $2,455 | $9,950 | $14,910 |
| QDWI | $5,405 | $7,299 | $4,000 | $6,000 |

Medicare notes under each table that income limits are slightly higher in Alaska and Hawaii, and it says the limits go up each year.

In the resource columns, QMB, SLMB and QI share the same limit. A single person needs counted resources below $9,950 for any of the three, and a married couple needs them below $14,910. What separates the three programs is income. The SLMB monthly income limit for an individual is $266 higher than the QMB limit ($1,616 minus $1,350), and the QI limit is another $200 higher ($1,816 minus $1,616). For married couples the steps are $360 (from $1,824 to $2,184) and $271 (from $2,184 to $2,455).

Put another way, the federal tables let an individual's monthly income run $466 above the QMB limit and still fall under the QI limit, and a couple's run $631 above the QMB limit. A person can be over the line for the most generous program and still be in range for one that pays the Part B premium.

The resource limit works differently. Because it is the same across QMB, SLMB and QI, a household above $9,950 or $14,910 in counted resources is over the federal resource limit for all three at once. That makes the resource question worth getting right: it decides whether the income tiers matter at all under the federal figures.

QDWI stands apart, with much higher income limits and much lower resource limits: $4,000 for an individual and $6,000 for a couple. It serves a narrow group, and most of this article is about the three programs that help with Part B.

## What counts toward the $9,950 limit

The phrase "resource limit" is easy to misread as a cap on what is in the bank. It is a cap on counted resources, and Medicare's page spells out which assets fall on each side of the line in a help panel titled "What counts in resource limits?"

| Counted as a resource | Not counted by states |
|---|---|
| Money in a checking account | Your home |
| Money in a savings account | One car |
| Money in a retirement account | Burial plot |
| Stocks | Up to $1,500 for burial expenses, if you have put that money aside |
| Bonds | Furniture |
| | Other household and personal items |

Several things follow from that list.

The $9,950 figure is a total, not a per-account limit. A person with $5,000 in checking and $5,000 in savings has $10,000 in counted resources, even though neither account alone is near the limit. Splitting money across accounts or banks does not change the sum.

The largest asset many retirees own, their home, is on the not-counted side. So is one car. A homeowner with a paid-off house and a car can still have counted resources well under $9,950, because neither of those appears in the total.

The burial exclusion has a condition attached. Medicare's wording is "Up to $1,500 for burial expenses if you have put that money aside." The words "put that money aside" matter. Medicare's page does not say how a state wants that money held or documented, so that is a question for your state Medicaid office when you apply. A burial plot is listed separately, so the plot itself is not counted either.

Everyday possessions are excluded. Furniture and "other household and personal items" are not counted, so a sofa or a set of dishes never enters the total.

The same counted and not-counted lists appear on Medicare's Extra Help page for the drug-cost program, so the resource definitions line up across the two forms of help even though the dollar limits differ.

## Retirement accounts, stocks and bonds

Retirement accounts are on the counted side of Medicare's list, and that is easy to overlook. Many savers think of an IRA or a workplace plan as money that is locked away until later, and so not really "available." Medicare's list does not make that distinction. It puts "money in a checking, savings, or retirement account" in the same line.

For a household whose savings are mostly in a retirement account, that can be the deciding fact. Someone with $2,000 in checking and a $9,000 retirement account has $11,000 in counted resources under that list, which is over $9,950, even though the checking balance alone looks small.

Stocks and bonds are on the counted list as well. That covers holdings people sometimes forget when they tally up savings: a few shares inherited years ago, or savings bonds in a drawer. If they are stocks or bonds, Medicare's list counts them.

What the Medicare page does not spell out is how a state values each of these assets, or whether it treats any specific type of account differently. It says only that some states don't count certain types or specific amounts of resources. That is a real gap in what the federal page can tell you, and it is one reason the page sends people to their state. If most of your counted resources sit in a retirement account, ask the state Medicaid office how it treats that account before deciding whether to apply. Better still, apply and let the state make the determination, which is what Medicare recommends.

## Worked example: a single retiree near the line

Take a single person in 2026 with these assets:

- Checking account: $3,400
- Savings account: $4,800
- IRA: $2,900
- Money set aside for burial expenses: $1,500
- A home and one car

Apply Medicare's list. The checking, savings and IRA balances count. The burial money, up to $1,500, does not count if it has been set aside, and the home and car do not count.

Counted resources: $3,400 + $4,800 + $2,900 = $11,100.

Federal resource limit for QMB, SLMB and QI: $9,950.

Difference: $11,100 − $9,950 = $1,150 over the federal limit.

Without the IRA, the count would be $3,400 + $4,800 = $8,200, which is $1,750 under the limit. The retirement account is what puts this person over the federal figure.

This example is about how the counting works, not a suggestion to move or spend money. Three facts from Medicare's pages matter more for this person than the $1,150 gap.

First, the state may not use the federal limit. Medicare says you may still qualify in your state even if your resources are higher than the federal limits. Contacting the state tells you which rules it uses, and applying gets you an official determination.

Second, the Extra Help resource limit is higher. For an individual it is $18,090, and $11,100 is $6,990 below it ($18,090 − $11,100). If the person's income also fits the Extra Help income limit, help with drug costs may still be available even if the state denies an MSP.

Third, the value of the premium help is large relative to the gap. At $202.90 a month, the standard Part B premium comes to $202.90 × 12 = $2,434.80 for a full year. That is the amount at stake in the MSP decision for one person paying the standard premium, before counting any deductibles or coinsurance that QMB would also cover.

The point of the arithmetic is to show where the line actually falls. A person who had looked only at a bank balance of $8,200 might have assumed either that they were safely under or that "having savings" disqualified them. Neither is a reliable shortcut. The total of counted resources, compared with the limit your state uses, is what decides the question.

## Worked example: a married couple and the Part B math

Now a married couple, both on Medicare, with:

- Joint checking: $2,600
- Joint savings: $7,400
- Bonds: $3,000
- A home, one car and household furniture

Counted resources: $2,600 + $7,400 + $3,000 = $13,000.

Federal resource limit for a married couple: $14,910.

Difference: $14,910 − $13,000 = $1,910 under the limit.

So the couple passes the federal resource test. The next question is income. Suppose the state counts the couple's income at $2,100 a month. Compare that with the federal married-couple income limits:

- QMB: $1,824. The couple is $2,100 − $1,824 = $276 over.
- SLMB: $2,184. The couple is $2,184 − $2,100 = $84 under.
- QI: $2,455. The couple is also under this one.

Under the federal figures, then, this couple would fit SLMB, which pays Part B premiums only. The state decides which program applies, and its rules on what income counts can change the result, but the federal tables point to SLMB.

The value of that help: two standard Part B premiums cost 2 × $202.90 = $405.80 a month, or $405.80 × 12 = $4,869.60 a year at the 2026 rate. Both members of the couple would also get Extra Help automatically, because SLMB is one of the programs Medicare names as bringing Extra Help with it.

The couple's margins are narrow. They are $1,910 under the resource limit and only $84 under the SLMB income limit. A small change in income could move them from one tier to another, or out of range under the federal figures. Medicare says the limits go up each year, so the margins are worth rechecking annually, and QI in particular requires a new application every year.

## When state rules are more generous than the federal limits

The figures in the tables above are federal limits. Medicare's page is explicit that a state's rules can be more generous: "You may still qualify for these programs in your state even if your income or resources are higher than the federal limits listed. Some states don't count certain types or specific amounts of income or resources when deciding who qualifies."

A shorter version, "You may qualify in other states for these programs even if your income or resources are higher than the federal limits listed," appears under each of the four program tables, followed by "Contact your state to find out." The statement has three practical consequences for someone weighing whether to apply.

A household over $9,950 or $14,910 is not necessarily out. The single retiree in the first example was $1,150 over the federal limit. In a state that does not count a certain type of resource, or counts only part of it, the result could be different. Medicare's page does not list each state's rules, and this article does not either. Contact your state Medicaid office to ask which resource exclusions apply.

The income test can also differ by state. The same sentence covers "certain types or specific amounts of income." A state may leave some income out of the count, which can move a household from one program tier to another.

The state decides. Medicare says that when you apply, "your state determines which program(s) you qualify for." Running the federal numbers is a good way to understand where you stand, but it is not a substitute for the state's decision.

Put together, these points support the instruction Medicare gives near the top of its page: even if you don't think you qualify, you should still apply. A household that assumes its savings disqualify it, and never applies, gives up the chance to have the state check that assumption against rules that may be more favorable than the federal ones.

## Extra Help: the higher $18,090 limit and the automatic link

Extra Help is Medicare's program for people with limited income and resources that lowers prescription drug costs. It is separate from the Medicare Savings Programs, with its own limits, but the two are connected.

The connection runs one way automatically. The Extra Help page lists three groups who get it without a separate application: people with full-benefit Medicaid coverage, people who get help from their state paying Part B premiums through a Medicare Savings Program, and people who get Supplemental Security Income payments from Social Security. The MSP page confirms it under each Part B program: QMB, SLMB and QI enrollees "also get Extra Help paying for your prescription drugs," and they pay no more than $12.65 in 2026 for each drug covered by their Medicare drug plan.

The Extra Help limits are higher than the MSP limits, especially on the resource side.

| 2026 limit | QMB, SLMB and QI | Extra Help |
|---|---|---|
| Resource limit, individual | $9,950 | $18,090 |
| Resource limit, married couple | $14,910 | $36,100 |
| Income limit, individual | $1,350 to $1,816 a month, by program | $23,940 |
| Income limit, married couple | $1,824 to $2,455 a month, by program | $32,460 |

One caution on the income rows: Medicare labels the MSP income limits as monthly, but its Extra Help table lists $23,940 and $32,460 with no monthly label, so those two figures should not be read against a monthly check the way the MSP limits are.

The resource gap is wide. An individual can have $18,090 − $9,950 = $8,140 more in counted resources under the Extra Help limit than under the federal MSP limit. For a married couple the difference is $36,100 − $14,910 = $21,190.

So a household over the MSP resource limit may still be under the Extra Help limit, as the single retiree in the first example was. And a household that qualifies for QMB, SLMB or QI doesn't need to clear the Extra Help test separately, because help from the state with Part B premiums brings Extra Help with it.

To put the $12.65 cap in concrete terms: a person with four drugs on their plan's covered list would pay no more than $12.65 for each, so at most 4 × $12.65 = $50.60 for one fill of all four, under the 2026 cap Medicare states for MSP enrollees.

The Extra Help page adds a few rules that matter to people whose income or resources change:

- Even if your income changes in the middle of the year, you keep getting Extra Help through Dec. 31.
- If you don't qualify now, you can reapply any time if your income and resources change.
- You can apply for Extra Help and Medicare Savings Programs at the same time. The page says Social Security will send information to your state to start an MSP application unless you tell it not to on the Extra Help application.
- You can contact your local State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP) for free help applying.

The third point is useful for anyone unsure where to start. An Extra Help application can open the door to an MSP application as well, so one filing can also start the state's review of MSP eligibility.

## QI reapplication and the first-come rule

Of the three programs that pay Part B premiums, QI has the highest income limits, and Medicare's page attaches three conditions to it.

You must apply every year to stay in the QI program. If the annual application is missed, the QI help can stop.

States approve QI applications on a first-come, first-served basis, with priority given to people who got QI benefits the previous year. Medicare's page does not give a deadline or say how quickly a state's QI slots fill, so the practical takeaway is simply that timing can matter, and a current QI enrollee should not let the renewal slide.

QI is only available for people who don't qualify for any other Medicaid coverage or benefits. The page adds that such a person "may qualify for help from another Medicare Savings Program." In other words, the state may determine that you qualify for QMB or SLMB instead.

For a household whose monthly income is above the federal SLMB limit ($1,616 for an individual, $2,184 for a couple) but not above the QI limit ($1,816 or $2,455), and that meets the other conditions, those rules are the reason to keep track of the annual application. Under a first-come rule, the order in which applications reach the state can matter.

## Applying through your state around Open Enrollment

The calendar is a natural trigger for this review. The Medicare Open Enrollment Period runs Oct. 15 to Dec. 7. During it you can join, drop or switch Medicare Advantage plans, switch between Original Medicare and Medicare Advantage, and join, drop or switch a Medicare drug plan if you're in Original Medicare. Coverage changes take effect Jan. 1 of the next year, and the plan must get your request to join by Dec. 7. For 2026's window, that means changes made by Dec. 7, 2026, start Jan. 1, 2027.

Medicare Savings Programs are not part of that window. They are run by your state, and Medicare's instruction is simply "Contact your state to apply." Nothing on Medicare's MSP page ties the application to the Oct. 15 to Dec. 7 dates. Open Enrollment is a good reminder to check, not a deadline for the state program.

The two do interact. Medicare's enrollment page lists getting Medicaid, or getting Extra Help to pay drug costs, among the situations that can give you a Special Enrollment Period for joining or switching plans. And the Extra Help page says that if you qualify for Extra Help, Medicare will enroll you in a Medicare drug plan if you don't already have one, and you can pick a different plan if you want.

A practical sequence for someone reviewing costs this fall:

1. List every account and holding that Medicare's page counts: checking, savings, retirement accounts, stocks and bonds. Use current balances.
2. Add them up and compare the total with $9,950 for an individual or $14,910 for a married couple. Then compare it with the Extra Help limits of $18,090 and $36,100.
3. Note what you have that does not count: your home, one car, a burial plot, up to $1,500 set aside for burial, furniture and household items.
4. Look at monthly income against the QMB, SLMB and QI limits, keeping in mind the state decides what income counts.
5. Contact your state Medicaid office to apply, even if you are over the federal figures. Medicare says to apply even if you don't think you qualify.
6. If you are in QI now, put the annual reapplication on your calendar.
7. Use Open Enrollment for the separate job of comparing health and drug plans for Jan. 1.

Having statements for each counted account at hand makes step 1 faster and gives the state the same numbers you used. A local SHIP can help with the Extra Help application at no cost, according to Medicare's Extra Help page.

## Common questions

**Does money in a retirement account count toward the Medicare Savings Program resource limit?**

Medicare's list of counted resources includes "money in a checking, savings, or retirement account," so under the federal definition it does. That surprises many people who think of retirement money as unavailable until later. Medicare's page also says some states don't count certain types or specific amounts of resources. Ask your state Medicaid office how it treats your account, and apply to get a determination rather than assuming.

**Is my house or car counted against the $9,950 limit?**

No, not under the list Medicare publishes. States don't count your home or one car, and they also don't count a burial plot, up to $1,500 set aside for burial expenses, furniture, or other household and personal items. That means a homeowner can have significant property and still be under the federal resource limit if their counted assets are small. The counted side is money in checking, savings and retirement accounts, plus stocks and bonds.

**What if my savings are a little over $9,950 or $14,910?**

You may still qualify. Medicare says you may qualify in your state even if your income or resources are higher than the federal limits, because some states don't count certain types or amounts of resources. Medicare's advice is to apply even if you don't think you qualify. Separately, the Extra Help resource limits are higher, at $18,090 for an individual and $36,100 for a married couple, so help with drug costs may be within reach even if an MSP is not.

**Do I have to wait for Open Enrollment to apply for a Medicare Savings Program?**

No. Medicare Savings Programs are run by states, and Medicare's instruction is to contact your state to apply; its page does not limit the application to the Oct. 15 to Dec. 7 window. Open Enrollment is for joining, dropping or switching Medicare Advantage and drug plans. Extra Help can also be reapplied for any time your income and resources change.

**If I qualify for QMB, SLMB or QI, do I also need to apply for Extra Help?**

Medicare lists people who get help from their state paying Part B premiums through a Medicare Savings Program among those who get Extra Help automatically. The MSP page says QMB, SLMB and QI enrollees also get Extra Help and pay no more than $12.65 in 2026 for each drug covered by their Medicare drug plan. Medicare's Extra Help page says you'll get a notice in the mail about your Extra Help. If your costs at the pharmacy don't match, the same page says to contact your drug plan, which may ask for proof that you get Extra Help.

**Will the limits change for next year?**

Medicare's page says the MSP limits go up each year, and its Extra Help page says those limits may go up each year. The figures above are the 2026 limits Medicare publishes; the next year's numbers were not on the pages reviewed for this article. The Part B premium can also change each year. The $12.65 per-drug figure is a 2026 amount, and Medicare's Extra Help page already lists different per-prescription amounts for 2027. Check Medicare.gov and your state Medicaid office for the current figures before you apply.

title: Savings Interest and the Jan. 15, 2027 Estimated Tax: The $1,000 Test
description: Big 2026 savings interest and no withholding? Run the $1,000 test and 90%/100%/110% safe harbors, then pick a W-4 change, a Jan. 15 payment or Jan. 31 filing.
content:
A saver who moved a large cash balance into a high-yield account or a run of CDs this year may be looking at thousands of dollars of 2026 interest with nothing set aside for the tax on it. Wages come with withholding; savings interest generally does not, and the IRS lists interest among the kinds of income that can call for estimated tax payments. Three of the four 2026 installment dates have already passed. In short: if you expect to owe at least $1,000 for 2026 after withholding and credits, and your withholding and credits will fall short of the smaller of 90% of your 2026 tax or 100% of your 2025 tax (110% if your 2025 AGI was more than $150,000, or $75,000 if you are married filing separately for 2026), you have an estimated tax requirement. Three options remain: a payment by Friday, Jan. 15, 2027, more withholding from your remaining 2026 paychecks, or filing the full return by Jan. 31, 2027, and paying the balance with it. Only the withholding route can reach back to the April, June and September periods, because of how the IRS dates each kind of payment.

The rules come from five IRS pages. [Publication 505 (2026), Tax Withholding and Estimated Tax](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p505) sets the thresholds, due dates and the January filing alternative. The IRS [Estimated taxes](https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/estimated-taxes) page states the same tests in shorter form and names interest as a trigger. The [Instructions for Form 2210 (2025)](https://www.irs.gov/instructions/i2210) explain how withholding is dated and how payments are applied when the penalty is figured. The news release [Interest rates remain the same for the fourth quarter of 2026](https://www.irs.gov/newsroom/interest-rates-remain-the-same-for-the-fourth-quarter-of-2026) gives the current underpayment rate. And [About Form 1040-ES](https://www.irs.gov/forms-pubs/about-form-1040-es) is where the payment form and its corrections are posted. This is general information about how the rules work, not advice on any individual return.

## Why savings interest creates an estimated tax gap

The federal system expects tax to be paid during the year. The Estimated taxes page puts it plainly: "Taxes must be paid as you earn or receive income during the year, either through withholding or estimated tax payments." It then names where withholding tends to fall short: "If the amount of income tax withheld from your salary or pension is not enough, or if you receive income such as interest, dividends, alimony, self-employment income, capital gains, prizes and awards, you may have to make estimated tax payments."

A salaried saver's withholding was most likely set up around wages. When interest grows from a few hundred dollars to several thousand in one year, withholding does not follow, and the tax on the extra interest builds up as a balance due. That is a gap, not yet a penalty. It becomes a penalty problem only if the shortfall crosses the thresholds below and nothing is done before the deadlines.

Two related topics are covered elsewhere on this site. Publication 505 notes that backup withholding "can apply to most kinds of payments that are reported on Form 1099," including interest; that separate mechanism is explained in [this site's post on backup withholding on savings interest](/2026/09/21/backup-withholding-on-savings-interest-why-the-bank-took-24/). Which year CD interest counts in, including interest on a multiyear CD you cannot yet withdraw, is covered in [Why you owe tax on a 5-year CD you cannot touch yet](/2026/09/25/why-you-owe-tax-on-a-5-year-cd-you-cannot-touch-yet/). This post starts from the point where you know your 2026 interest and need to know whether the tax on it must be paid before you file.

## The two tests and the 110% rule

Publication 505 states the general rule in two parts. You must pay estimated tax for 2026 if both apply:

1. "You expect to owe at least $1,000 in tax for 2026 after subtracting your withholding and tax credits."
2. "You expect your withholding and tax credits to be less than the smaller of: 90% of the tax to be shown on your 2026 tax return, or 100% of the tax shown on your 2025 tax return. Your 2025 tax return must cover all 12 months."

Both must be true. A saver who will owe $3,000 at filing, is not subject to the 110% rule below, and whose withholding already covers 100% of last year's tax fails the second test and has no estimated tax requirement under this rule, even though a balance will be due in April. A saver well short of last year's tax who will owe only $600 fails the first test.

For savers, the details matter.

**The $1,000 is tax, not income.** Interest of $1,000 triggers nothing by itself. The question is whether your 2026 tax, after subtracting withholding and credits, reaches $1,000. Publication 505's flowchart adds: "Don't subtract any estimated tax payments."

**The prior-year test is already fixed.** It uses the tax shown on the 2025 return, which does not move when 2026 interest goes up. For a saver whose income jumped this year, that fixed number is often the easier target because it is smaller than 90% of the new, higher 2026 tax.

**"Whichever is smaller" works in your favor.** The Estimated taxes page frames it the same way: most taxpayers avoid the penalty if they paid "at least 90% of the tax for the current year, or 100% of the tax shown on the return for the prior year, whichever is smaller." Once withholding and credits reach the lower figure, the general rule no longer requires estimated payments, however much interest arrives late in the year.

Higher-income households get a tougher prior-year target. Publication 505 says: "If your AGI for 2025 was more than $150,000 ($75,000 if your filing status for 2026 is Married filing a separate return), substitute 110% for 100%" in the prior-year part of the general rule. It names the line: "For 2025, AGI is the amount shown on Form 1040 or 1040-SR, line 11b." The test looks at 2025 AGI, so a household that first crosses $150,000 this year because of interest still uses 100% for 2026. The trigger is "more than," so AGI of exactly $150,000 stays at 100% unless you are married filing separately. And the $75,000 line depends on 2026 filing status, not 2025.

There is also a full exemption. You don't have to pay estimated tax for 2026 if you had no tax liability for 2025, were a U.S. citizen or resident alien for the whole year, and your 2025 tax year covered a 12-month period. Publication 505 defines no tax liability as a 2025 total tax of zero, or not having been required to file. Someone who had little income last year and lives on savings interest this year should check that first. Special rules apply to farmers and fishermen; they are outside this post.

| Your situation | Prior-year target | Current-year target | Withholding and credits must reach |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2025 AGI of $150,000 or less (not married filing separately) | 100% of 2025 tax | 90% of 2026 tax | The smaller of the two |
| 2025 AGI more than $150,000 | 110% of 2025 tax | 90% of 2026 tax | The smaller of the two |
| Married filing separately for 2026, 2025 AGI more than $75,000 | 110% of 2025 tax | 90% of 2026 tax | The smaller of the two |
| No 2025 tax liability, citizen or resident all year, 12-month 2025 tax year | Not applicable | Not applicable | No estimated tax required |
| Expect to owe less than $1,000 after withholding and credits | Not applicable | Not applicable | No estimated tax required |

Source: Publication 505 (2026).

## Worked example: a saver under the $150,000 line

The numbers here are hypothetical and chosen to keep the arithmetic easy to follow.

A single filer moved $200,000 into savings early in 2026. At a hypothetical 4.5% yield, that produces $9,000 of interest for the year: $200,000 × 0.045 = $9,000. The 2025 return shows total tax of $14,000 and AGI of $120,000, so the 100% target applies. A projection for 2026, including the interest, shows total tax of $16,000. Withholding for all of 2026 is projected at $13,000.

**Test 1:** $16,000 − $13,000 = $3,000 expected at filing. That is at least $1,000, so the test is met.

**Test 2:**

- 90% of 2026 tax: $16,000 × 0.90 = $14,400
- 100% of 2025 tax: $14,000
- The smaller amount is $14,000, and $13,000 of withholding falls short of it.

Both tests are met, so estimated tax is required. The shortfall against the safe harbor is $14,000 − $13,000 = $1,000. That is not the $3,000 the filer will owe. The rule only asks the filer to reach the safe harbor during the year; the other $2,000 can be paid with the return without triggering the estimated tax rules, as long as the $14,000 target is met in time.

Now spread the target across the year. Publication 505 says the regular installment method divides the annual amount by 4, and the Form 2210 instructions say that for most taxpayers the required installment is "one-fourth of the required annual payment."

- Required installment per period: $14,000 ÷ 4 = $3,500
- Withholding credited per period: $13,000 ÷ 4 = $3,250
- Shortfall per period: $3,500 − $3,250 = $250
- Four periods × $250 = $1,000

That per-period view decides which fix works best.

## Where the 2026 calendar stands now

Publication 505 lists the 2026 payment periods and due dates. Three are in the past.

| Payment period | 2026 due date | Status on Oct. 7, 2026 |
|---|---|---|
| Jan. 1 – March 31 | April 15, 2026 | Passed |
| April 1 – May 31 | June 15, 2026 | Passed |
| June 1 – Aug. 31 | Sept. 15, 2026 | Passed |
| Sept. 1 – Dec. 31 | Jan. 15, 2027 | Open |

Source: Publication 505 (2026).

Publication 505's Table 2-1 adds that if income subject to estimated tax first arises "After Aug. 31," the only payment is due Jan. 15 of the next year.

The publication is clear that "The penalty is figured separately for each payment period," and it warns: "If you figure your payments using the regular installment method and later refigure your payments because of an increase in income, you may be charged a penalty for underpayment of estimated tax for the period(s) before you changed your payments."

For a saver who has made no estimated payments, that warning applies directly. Paying everything on Jan. 15 handles the fourth period but does not reach back to April, June or September. The Form 2210 instructions explain how late money is treated: "Your payments are applied first to any underpayment balance on an earlier installment even if you designate a payment for a later period," and "The penalty is figured for the number of days that each underpayment remains unpaid." A January payment ends the clock on earlier shortfalls; it does not erase the time they were outstanding.

If a due date falls on a Saturday, Sunday or legal holiday, Publication 505 says a payment is on time if made on the next day that isn't one. Jan. 15, 2027, is a Friday.

## Why more withholding can cover earlier quarters

Withholding is dated differently from estimated payments, and for anyone with a paycheck this is the most useful rule in the whole topic.

The Form 2210 instructions state: "For withheld federal income tax and excess social security or tier 1 RRTA, you are considered to have paid one-fourth of these amounts on each payment due date unless you can show otherwise."

Withholding from a December paycheck is not treated as a December payment. By default it is spread evenly across all four 2026 due dates, including the three that have passed. An estimated payment is dated the day it is made.

Back to the worked example, with $250 short in each period:

**Fix 1: a $1,000 estimated payment on Jan. 15, 2027.** Applied first to the earliest shortfall, it leaves the April 15 shortfall of $250 unpaid from April 15, 2026, to Jan. 15, 2027. The June and September shortfalls stay unpaid from their own due dates to Jan. 15. Only the fourth $250 is on time.

**Fix 2: an extra $1,000 of withholding from the remaining 2026 paychecks.** Total withholding becomes $13,000 + $1,000 = $14,000. Treated as paid one-fourth on each due date, that is $14,000 ÷ 4 = $3,500 per period, which equals the $3,500 required installment. Shortfall per period: $0.

The same $1,000 clears all four periods. Both IRS pages also describe the employer route for wage earners. The Estimated taxes page says: "If you receive salaries and wages, you can avoid having to pay estimated tax by asking your employer to withhold more tax from your earnings. To do this, file a new Form W-4 with your employer. There is a special line on Form W-4 for you to enter the additional amount you want your employer to withhold." It also points to the IRS Tax Withholding Estimator for checking the amount.

Practical notes on this route:

- **The payroll calendar limits it.** The extra amount has to come out of 2026 paychecks. Divide the target by the pay dates left and enter that per-paycheck figure on the new W-4. A W-4 filed in late December may reach one paycheck or none.
- **The default helps.** The Form 2210 instructions let you date withholding by when it was actually withheld instead, but that is an election: "If you treat withholding as paid on the dates it was actually withheld for estimated tax purposes, you must check box D in Part II and complete and attach Form 2210 to your return." Someone adding withholding late in the year generally benefits from the even-spread default.
- **Pensions count too.** The Estimated taxes page refers to tax "withheld from your salary or pension," and the Form 2210 rule covers withheld federal income tax in general. Publication 505 explains that pension withholding is set by the Form W-4P (or similar form) you gave the payer and stays in effect unless you submit a new Form W-4P, so a retiree can raise it with a new form.

## Paying by Jan. 15 or filing by Jan. 31

Publication 505 offers a second way to handle the fourth installment: "If you file your 2026 Form 1040 or 1040-SR by January 31, 2027, and pay the rest of the tax you owe, you don't need to make the payment due on January 15, 2027."

Its example: "You do not pay any estimated tax for 2026. You file the 2026 income tax return and pay the balance due shown on the return on January 26, 2027. Your estimated tax for the fourth payment period is considered to have been paid on time. However, you may owe a penalty for not making the first three estimated tax payments, if required. Any penalty for not making those payments will be figured up to January 26, 2027."

So this route replaces the Jan. 15 payment and stops the clock on the first three periods when you file and pay. It requires a complete return and full payment, and it does not cure those earlier periods.

For savers, the obstacle is paperwork. Filing by Jan. 31 means having accurate figures for all 2026 income, including interest from every account, in the last weeks of January. If you won't have those numbers by late January, the Jan. 15 payment is the more workable path. Also note that Jan. 31, 2027, falls on a Sunday, and Publication 505's weekend rule is written for estimated payment due dates. Anyone relying on this alternative should file a few days early rather than test how the weekend date is treated.

For the Jan. 15 payment itself, the Estimated taxes page says: "You may send estimated tax payments with Form 1040-ES by mail, or you can pay online, by phone or from your mobile device using the IRS app," and you can pay through your online account, "where you can see your payment history." Anyone mailing a voucher should check the About Form 1040-ES page, which lists a "Correction to the mailing addresses in the 2026 Form 1040-ES -- 23-FEB-2026" and a "Correction to state and local income tax deduction amount in the 2026 Form 1040-ES -- 25-FEB-2026." A copy saved before late February may not reflect them.

| Route | What it covers | Main requirement | Main limit |
|---|---|---|---|
| Extra withholding from remaining 2026 pay | All four periods, one-fourth each by default | A paycheck or pension with withholding | Limited by pay dates left in 2026 |
| Estimated payment by Jan. 15, 2027 | Fourth period on time; applied first to earlier shortfalls | Payment by the due date | Earlier shortfalls count as unpaid until paid |
| File and pay all tax by Jan. 31, 2027 | Fourth period treated as paid on time | Complete return and full payment | Earlier shortfalls count as unpaid until filing; needs all forms early |
| Annualized income installment method | Can lower required installments for early periods | Form 2210 with the return | More calculation; depends on when income arrived |

Sources: Publication 505 (2026); Instructions for Form 2210 (2025).

The routes can be combined, such as extra withholding plus a smaller Jan. 15 payment.

## Interest that arrived late: the annualized method

The regular installment method assumes income arrives evenly; Publication 505 says to use it "only if your income is basically the same throughout the year." Savings interest often doesn't. Interest on a new account builds only after the deposit, so money moved into savings partway through the year produces most of its interest in the later months. (Which year CD interest belongs to is a separate question, covered in the CD post linked above.)

For uneven income, Publication 505 describes the annualized income installment method, which "annualizes your tax at the end of each period based on a reasonable estimate of your income, deductions, and other items relating to events that occurred from the beginning of the tax year through the end of the period." The Estimated taxes page summarizes the benefit: "if your income is received unevenly during the year, you may be able to avoid or lower the penalty by annualizing your income and making unequal payments."

Each installment is measured against income from Jan. 1 through the end of that period: March 31, May 31, Aug. 31 and Dec. 31. Interest that showed up after Aug. 31 sits outside the first three measuring periods. That has two effects:

- **Early installments can be smaller.** If most of the year's interest came in the fall, the tax figured on income through August can be lower than an even one-fourth share, and the required installments for those periods shrink.
- **The late income still has to be covered.** The method shifts the requirement to the period in which the income arrived, which for late-year interest is the Jan. 15 period.

The method adds paperwork. Publication 505: "If you use the annualized income installment method to figure your estimated tax payments, you must file Form 2210 with your 2026 tax return." In the Form 2210 instructions the method is Schedule AI, and they say it "may be to your benefit to figure your required installments by using the annualized income installment method."

One pattern where annualizing helps is little extra income in the first eight months and most of it after. It generally does less for someone whose interest built steadily from January, because that income was present in every period. For that saver, extra withholding is usually the cleaner fix.

## Worked example: no withholding to adjust

Also hypothetical. A retired single filer lives on savings and has no paycheck and no withholding. The 2025 return shows total tax of $6,000 and AGI under $150,000. Projected 2026 tax is $9,000. No estimated payments have been made.

**Test 1:** $9,000 − $0 = $9,000 owed after withholding, which is at least $1,000.

**Test 2:** 90% of 2026 tax is $9,000 × 0.90 = $8,100. 100% of 2025 tax is $6,000. The smaller is $6,000, and $0 of withholding falls short.

Estimated tax is required. Under the regular method, each installment is $6,000 ÷ 4 = $1,500.

| Due date | Required | Paid by due date | Shortfall |
|---|---|---|---|
| April 15, 2026 | $1,500 | $0 | $1,500 |
| June 15, 2026 | $1,500 | $0 | $1,500 |
| Sept. 15, 2026 | $1,500 | $0 | $1,500 |
| Jan. 15, 2027 | $1,500 | Depends on route | Depends on route |

The first three shortfalls total $1,500 × 3 = $4,500, and they already exist. With no withholding to spread, nothing done in October can backdate a payment. What the filer still controls:

- **Pay sooner rather than later.** Because penalty time runs for "the number of days that each underpayment remains unpaid," paying the $4,500 now instead of in January shortens the count for all three periods. The Estimated taxes page notes that paying weekly, biweekly or monthly is fine "as long as you've paid enough in by the end of the quarter."
- **Cover the fourth installment** by Jan. 15, 2027, or file and pay everything by Jan. 31, 2027.
- **Check Schedule AI** if most of the 2026 interest arrived late in the year.

This post does not put a dollar figure on any penalty; the Form 2210 worksheet for the 2026 return does that.

## What the 7% rate means for waiting

The IRS sets its interest rates quarterly. For the quarter that began Oct. 1, 2026, it announced that rates would stay the same: "For individuals, the rate for overpayments and underpayments will be 7% per year, compounded daily." The release explains the formula: "For taxpayers other than corporations, the overpayment and underpayment rate is the federal short-term rate plus 3 percentage points," computed "from the federal short-term rate determined during July 2026."

The Form 2210 instructions describe the penalty worksheet as "applying the appropriate rate against each underpayment" for the days it remains unpaid. In the 2025 worksheet, each rate period's line multiplies the underpayment by the number of days, divided by 365, and by that period's rate. The rate is applied separately to each rate period an underpayment spans.

That makes the cost of a shortfall depend on time and on the rate for each period it spans. A shortfall from April 15 that is paid in October has run for fewer days than the same shortfall paid on Jan. 15.

The money that could pay the tax often sits in the same high-yield account that created the problem. Leaving it there until April means weighing that account's yield against a penalty figured at the IRS rate for each period. Rates for later quarters are announced separately, so this post does not assume them.

## A decision checklist for October

A saver with substantial 2026 interest can work through these in order:

1. **Pull the 2025 numbers.** Total tax and AGI (Form 1040 or 1040-SR, line 11b). If AGI was more than $150,000, or more than $75,000 when married filing separately for 2026, the prior-year target is 110%.
2. **Check the no-liability exemption** described above.
3. **Project 2026 tax and withholding,** including all interest expected through Dec. 31.
4. **Run the two tests.** Is the expected balance after withholding and credits at least $1,000? Are withholding and credits below the smaller of 90% of 2026 tax and 100% or 110% of 2025 tax?
5. **Measure the gap against the safe harbor,** not the full balance due.
6. **Look at withholding if you have a paycheck or pension,** since it is treated as paid one-fourth on each due date by default.
7. **Cover what is left** with a Jan. 15 payment, or file and pay in full by Jan. 31, 2027.
8. **Consider Schedule AI** if the interest arrived mostly after Aug. 31.
9. **Reset withholding in January** if 2026 was a one-time spike.

Anyone with self-employment income, large capital gains or a filing status change should check with a tax professional, because the general rule is only one part of Publication 505.

## Common questions

**Does $1,000 of savings interest mean I have to pay estimated tax?**

No. The $1,000 threshold in Publication 505 applies to tax owed after withholding and credits, not to the amount of interest. A saver earning several thousand dollars of interest may still owe far less than $1,000 at filing if wage withholding covers most of the tax. Even with an expected balance of $1,000 or more, estimated tax is required only if withholding and credits also fall below the smaller of 90% of 2026 tax or 100% (or 110%) of 2025 tax.

**I missed the April, June and September dates. Can I still fix those quarters?**

Not with an estimated payment, because a payment is dated when it is made and is applied first to the earliest shortfall. Withholding works differently. The Form 2210 instructions treat withheld federal income tax as paid one-fourth on each due date unless you show otherwise. Adding withholding from your remaining 2026 paychecks can cover earlier periods in a way a January payment cannot.

**If I file early, do I still need to send the Jan. 15 payment?**

Not if you file your complete 2026 Form 1040 or 1040-SR by Jan. 31, 2027, and pay all the tax you owe, according to Publication 505. The fourth installment is then treated as paid on time. A penalty can still apply to the first three periods if those payments were required, figured up to the date you file and pay. Filing that early also means having accurate interest figures for every account.

**My 2025 AGI was just under $150,000. Do I use 100% or 110%?**

Publication 505 switches to 110% only if 2025 AGI was "more than $150,000," or more than $75,000 if your 2026 filing status is married filing separately. AGI at or below the line keeps the 100% figure. Check line 11b of your 2025 Form 1040 or 1040-SR, not projected 2026 income. A jump in 2026 interest does not change the multiplier for 2026.

**Should I use the annualized method?**

It is worth checking if most of your extra interest arrived late in the year. The method measures each installment against income through the end of that period, so interest received after Aug. 31 does not raise earlier installments. It requires attaching Form 2210 with Schedule AI to your 2026 return. If your interest built up evenly from January, it usually changes little, and extra withholding or a prompt payment is simpler.

**Will the IRS tell me if I owe a penalty?**

Generally, yes. The Form 2210 instructions say the IRS will generally figure the penalty and send a bill, and that you should not file Form 2210 in that case. The exceptions include checking box B, C or D in Part II, such as when using the annualized method or dating withholding as actually withheld. A waiver can apply in limited circumstances listed on the Estimated taxes page, which points to the Form 2210 instructions for how to request one; those instructions say to check box A or box B in Part II, and with box A you attach only page 1 of Form 2210.

The prior-year target is fixed by last year's return, withholding can still be added from this year's pay, and both the Jan. 15 payment and the Jan. 31 filing alternative remain open. For shortfalls covered by a direct payment rather than withholding, the penalty count runs until the day the money is paid.
